entries.title: Francesca Hong Didn’t Run Broadcast Ads. Did It Cost Her Wisconsin?
entries.summary: The campaign’s decision to focus on digital platform advertising could have ultimately led to its demise, some strategists say.
entries.content:
Francesca Hong’s Wisconsin gubernatorial campaign embraced the new era of campaigning for progressive candidates, from a social media-dominated bid to her democratic socialist-influenced policy platform.

But part of her razor-thin loss to David Crowley on Tuesday could be explained by the traditional, or a lack thereof: broadcast TV ad spending.

Despite leading the Democratic field by double-digit margins before the primary, Hong was the only active candidate to seek the governorship without running broadcast TV ads, according to ad-tracking service AdImpact.

Some strategists think the Hong campaign’s decision to focus on digital platform advertising ultimately led to its demise, costing her key parts of the electorate.

“In a primary, voters are more persuadable,” Democratic strategist Jared Leopold told NOTUS. “Especially in a smaller primary, it's a mistake to try to narrow cast too much because you actually do need to hit a wider swath of a primary electorate, because more people are likely to change their votes at the end than in a general election.”

The Democratic Socialist platform encourages disavowing certain large-dollar donors, meaning progressive candidates like Hong are working with a different set of funding than their opponents — even if rejecting corporate cash boosts them in the eyes of voters.

“This campaign is entirely people-funded: no corporate PACs,” the “About” section of her website says.

Hong’s opponents massively outspent her on advertising, regardless of the medium. Crowley — who briefly exited the race — reported $572,317 in media expenses, including $402,042 on TV ads, according to an analysis conducted by WisPolitics a week before the primary. He announced a six-figure TV buy when he reentered nine days later with the incumbent governor’s endorsement.

Republican Rep. Tom Tiffany, who Crowley will face in November, has already reported $7.6 million in media expenditures, including $3.9 million on TV.

Hong dedicated $150,200 to online ads, with nothing going to broadcast spots. Some of the only positive TV advertising for her campaign came from a super PAC tied to Republicans, which spent $2.2 million in an effort likely aimed at boosting her as an easier general election opponent for Tiffany — a common practice across both parties.

Her focus on digital spending tracks with the electorate of younger voters she was building, said Travis Ridout, co-director of the Wesleyan Media Project, which tracks national political ads. Hong opted for more casual and conversational digital ads than the flashier and highly edited political advertisements traditionally run on broadcast TV — perhaps in an attempt to capture voters from a “tuned out” portion of the electorate, Ridout said.

“When you're running a very progressive campaign, I think you're trying to find voters who might be disillusioned by the way things are going,” he told NOTUS.

“Those people might have dropped out of politics for a while, and thus you're not necessarily going to be finding them watching the local news at 6 p.m. on broadcast television,” he added.

Neither campaign commented for this story.

Like fellow Democratic Socialist Zohran Mamdani, Hong focused her ad buys on digital platforms and streaming services. But a few months before the New York City mayoral primary, Mamdani too eventually started running TV ads.

Exit polls show Hong won several counties helmed by colleges and certain cities like Green Bay, while Crowley swept the majority of Wisconsin’s rural districts, as well as Milwaukee County and its suburbs. Hong, however, appeared to overperform in rural counties in the state’s northwest — including St. Croix and Douglas — which also happen to sit in Minnesota media markets that saw fewer political ads on linear broadcast channels.

Even so, Hong’s lack of broadcast ads likely cost her blocs like older voters who can drive turnout, strategists say.

“It’s a mistake to not communicate with a part of the electorate,” Leopold said. “There’s still a lot of people, particularly older people, who watch a lot of TV.”

Because people crave authenticity in politics, digital ads that connect voters with the candidate in a positive way can stand out in an advertising environment defined by attack ads, Ridout said. But especially in a statewide race, “integrated campaigns that combine social media, CTV and broadcast” can make all the difference for candidates, he said.

“You can have targeted messages that only go to individuals, but sometimes all a campaign needs is name recognition,” Ridout said, adding that a blitz of broadcast ads can boost a candidate that much more. “People don’t vote for candidates they’ve never heard of before.”
entries.author: Jenna Monnin

entries.title: In Northern Virginia, a Confrontation With ICE Sparks Questions About Cameras and Transparency
entries.summary: The agents involved in the incident were wearing body cameras, but the footage may never be released.
entries.content:
The front- and rear-facing dashboard cameras that Carolina Molina has mounted on her Toyota Supra are, by her telling, for accountability.

“It’s for traffic incidents. I have a nice car, and if somebody were to hit me I want proof of that,” she said. “You just never know what could happen, so you should always protect yourself.”

But earlier this week, the dashcams became a tool for a different type of accountability.

On Monday, a masked ICE agent confronted Molina as she drove through an office park in the Bailey’s Crossroads area of Northern Virginia, pointing a gun at her head while accusing her of trying to run them over. She says he was lying, and had the dashcam footage to prove it.

Sign up for the NOTUS Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

Molina — a first-generation American whose family is from El Salvador — caught the rest of the interaction with her cellphone’s camera, and she posted the footage on Instagram.

The footage immediately went viral, prompting widespread criticism over the agent’s aggressive tactics and again pointing a spotlight at ICE, which came under intense scrutiny earlier this year for two killings in Minnesota and again this summer for similar fatalities in Texas and Maine.

The Department of Homeland Security is standing by the agents involved, accusing Molina in a statement of “weaponizing her vehicle against them — all in an attempt to help illegal aliens get away.” The agency also said Molina herself “could face criminal prosecution as a result of her actions.”

Democratic Rep. Suhas Subramanyam, who represents Virginia’s 10th Congressional District, is calling for criminal charges to be pressed against the agent, not Molina.

“They have no right to attack someone who exercises their First Amendment right to free speech,” he told NOTUS. “If ICE doesn’t want to have people jeer [at] them wherever they go, they should change their tactics. They should be more accountable, more transparent to the American people.”

But Patrick Jaicomo, an attorney specializing in police conduct for the libertarian Institute for Justice, says that accountability may be hard to come by.

“When you see federal agents violating someone’s rights, there should be an avenue to seek relief in court,” he says. “But there is very little to be done, and we’ve had to piece together novel theories to restore some avenue for federal accountability. The federal government has no interest in holding itself accountable no matter how egregious the behavior is.”

After ICE agents fatally shot two people in Minnesota in January, the uproar prompted DHS leaders to promise to outfit agents nationwide with body cameras, which advocates tout as one tool to ensure that there’s a record of when things go wrong. While that rollout hasn’t been completed, the agents who confronted Molina were wearing body cameras.

But whether the footage is released remains an open question. The Associated Press recently reported that the agency’s existing policy gives it full discretion over whether to release footage from body cameras, and specifies it will do so when “it is in the best interests of the agency.”

This conflicts with policies in many local law enforcement agencies, including D.C.’s Metropolitan Police Department, which mandate that footage showing a serious use of force be made public within five days of the incident — unless the victim or their family objects. (Earlier this year, the D.C. Council passed a bill expanding the release of footage to include situations where federal agents use serious force when patrolling with D.C. police officers. A group of Republican senators is now trying to repeal that law.)

An email to a DHS spokesperson inquiring as to whether the footage in Molina’s case would be released went unanswered. Molina said Wednesday she would like to see it made public, and Subramanyam said he plans to request the footage from DHS — but also that the agency’s existing policy troubles him.

“That policy makes clear that they don’t care about the American people; they only care about themselves and protecting the administration and its immigration overreach,” he said. “If they cared about our country and the American people, they would release body camera footage and all the other information related to an incident like this, so that everyone knew what was going on and exactly what happened, and we could fix the issue.”

Molina conceded that had she not been equipped to record the interaction, things could have ended much worse for her.

“I think they would have shot me and gotten away with it,” she said.

“Body cameras are a good thing,” Jaicomo said. “They are used in many cases to show the objective truth of what happened. They can show a criminal did criminal things or the police lied. In this case, it’s the latter. But if those videos are never recorded or made public, they serve no purpose.”

Another element of Molina’s incident was that the ICE agents were masked — as they have been through much of the Trump administration. Earlier this year, Virginia lawmakers approved a bill prohibiting federal agents from being masked, but it is currently held up in litigation. Democratic Virginia Sens. Mark Warner and Tim Kaine have introduced legislation to end masking by federal agents.

“There must be an increase in transparency, accountability, and safety in immigration law enforcement,” Warner said in an email to NOTUS. “My Immigration Enforcement Identification Act would make it illegal for law enforcement officers to obscure their faces and require that they clearly display their agency, name, and a unique identifier while conducting immigration enforcement functions. It also has some commonsense exceptions for select tactical missions and officer health and safety.”

For Subramanyam, Monday’s incident shows why some people want to scrap ICE altogether, he said. But he wouldn’t go that far.

“We do need to do immigration reform, but not like this. We do need to do immigration enforcement, but not like this,” he said. “What we need is a completely new way of doing immigration enforcement.”

As for Molina, a therapist by trade, she said she isn’t yet sure how she’ll proceed but that she will be speaking to an attorney. She wants the ICE agents who confronted her to be investigated, but absent that, she proposed her own form of accountability: “therapy.”

entries.title: Defense Lobbyists Brace for Democrats’ Oversight Blitz
entries.summary: “Industry will be stuck between a rock and a hard place,” one lobbyist said.
entries.content:
Democrats have spent two years seething that the Trump administration shut Congress out of decisions about the Pentagon, from the Iran war to politically connected contractors and a defense budget that’s ballooned to $1.5 trillion.

If the party prevails in the midterms, it will finally have the gavels and subpoena power to act.

K Street lobbyists say that if Democrats retake one or both chambers, they’re girding for aggressive investigations of President Donald Trump’s Pentagon and the companies that do business with it, particularly if the administration obstructs.

“You’re going to have a major focus on the department, but wherever or whenever they get stymied, or maybe even to build a case, they might bring in industry,” said John Keast, who heads Keast Strategic Solutions and works with major defense clients. “Industry will be stuck between a rock and a hard place because new leadership [in Congress] hasn’t changed who’s in the White House for two more years.”

Democrats already have a prime target. This week, Sen. Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut, the top Democrat on the Senate Investigations Subcommittee, was among lawmakers who asked the Pentagon’s inspector general to investigate reports that defense companies backed by 1789 Capital, where Donald Trump Jr. is an investor, and American Ventures, where Eric Trump is an investor, received billions of dollars in government awards. “We need to look into whether Trump’s sons are profiting from investments in defense contractors that involve insider information or contracts awarded in ways that compromise defense interests, among a number of issues,” Blumenthal said in an interview.Democrats should, Blumenthal said, probe the administration’s growing reliance on single-source contracts and whether the administration has given preferential treatment to companies with political ties, particularly those that donated to Trump’s White House ballroom project.

Potential conflicts are only one investigative lane. In the House, where Democrats are widely seen as having their best chance of winning, House Armed Services Democrats would likely begin with the Pentagon itself and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, whose handling of the unpopular Iran conflict, officer purges and deadly boat strikes have drawn sharp criticism.

The House Armed Services Committee would likely focus on military strategy, acquisition decisions and the Pentagon’s rapidly growing budget, former aides said. The House Oversight Committee, meanwhile, is more likely to go after politically charged questions involving potential corruption, conflicts of interest, companies connected to Trump allies such as SpaceX and other ethics issues.

Lobbyists are focused on the panel’s top Democrat, Rep. Adam Smith of Washington, who would become chairman if Democrats retake the House. They say Smith supports a strong defense industrial base but also that the Pentagon must justify its ever-growing budget, a perspective that could put some weapon programs on the chopping block.

"I think you will see pragmatic pushback" on the administration's defense spending plans, said Brian Greer, a former House Armed Services staffer who now heads Greer Strategic Partners. "Which programs are we using? Which ones need to be retired? Are sound budgetary decisions being made?"



The Iran war and its economic fallout have driven Democrats’ midterm messaging, with lawmakers arguing the administration has dragged the country into another lengthy Middle Eastern war while stonewalling Congress. Former aides say a Democratic victory would leave Smith and party leaders facing intense pressure from infuriated members to demand long-sought answers from the Pentagon.

The House Armed Services Committee has traditionally relied on voluntary cooperation from the Pentagon, rather than subpoenas. But former congressional aides expect Democrats to hold an array of hearings early in the new Congress and issue subpoenas if Pentagon officials are uncooperative.

“They are going to want him to get after the department and the president about Iran, about Ukraine, about extrajudicial killings; the list is long,” said one former committee aide who spoke on the condition of anonymity. “Here's where the problem is: They won't get answers from the Department of Defense.”

And that’s where industry could find itself pulled into the fight. If Pentagon officials stiff-arm congressional investigators, lawmakers could turn to testimony and documents from outside the government, including defense contractors and investors with close ties to the administration.

“My advice to companies right now is, if you don’t understand what it’s like to testify before Congress, you better learn pretty quick,” the former aide said. “If you have anything that you think is going to draw their ire, then you should start looking now for consultants who can help you prepare.”

Lobbyists expect Democrats to scrutinize the administration's equity stakes in private defense and mining companies. They also expect questions about marquee initiatives such as the Golden Dome — which Smith has called “a project no one can explain” — and the cost of retrofitting Qatar's donated aircraft for use as Air Force One.

Some firms are already expanding to meet that demand. Last month, the K Street firm Invariant hired David Weinberg, the former Democratic staff director of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, to lead its congressional oversight and investigations practice, aimed at helping clients prepare for heightened scrutiny.

Weinberg said companies should already be mapping out where they could face congressional attention and prepare responses. It’s not too soon for Democratic committee leaders, who he said are already thinking through staffing, investigative priorities and how they would use the larger budgets available to the majority.“I wouldn't be shocked to see some of the first oversight letters going in the first week of the new Congress,” Weinberg said. “I do think that you'll see chairs that are aggressive out of the gate.”

But Democrats face political risks, according to Michael Herson, the CEO of American Defense International, a consulting firm that focuses on government relations for major defense companies. While he expects aggressive oversight, he cautioned Democrats against letting investigations overshadow the need to address the economic issues that are driving voters.

“I think there's a chance that they could overreach,” Herson said. “At the end of the day, the ordinary American is going to wonder, how did all this oversight help improve my day-to-day cost of living? Democrats have to be careful not to make this the crux of their Congress.”

Wherever Democrats ultimately direct their gaze, lobbyists say companies cannot afford to wait and should keep their relationships with Democratic lawmakers from growing stale.

“The companies that are postured to be able to anticipate the House and Senate flip, if it happens, will be in a better position than the ones who have only worked with the R’s,” Greer said. “Democrats are sensitive to a Johnny-come-lately approach.”
